item.title: Slurm: fair-share, QOS and preemption
item.description:
Slurm

Slurm carries the batch workload and the guarantee. Reference numbers are [n] entries of the bibliography.

Fair-share principles

Multifactor priority

With PriorityType=priority/multifactor, a job’s priority is an integer: a site factor, plus the sum of each factor (age, association, fair-share, size, partition, QOS, TRES) times its weight, minus the nice value. Each factor is between 0 and 1 and weights default to 0, so only the configured factors count [2].

The Fair Tree algorithm

Fair Tree has been Slurm’s default since 19.05 [2]. At each level of the association tree it computes the Level Fairshare [1]:

LF = S / U S = S_self / S_(self+siblings) U = U_self / U_(self+siblings)

LF > 1 means under-served; LF < 1, over-served; LF = infinity with no consumption. Siblings are sorted by decreasing LF, the tree is walked depth first, and each user receives a rank. The user’s fair-share factor is rank / number of users: 1.0 for the first [1].

The decisive property for us: the first level compares A against B before looking at users. If A is over-served, all of B’s users come before all of A’s, whatever individual consumption is. This is exactly the wanted behaviour between two institutions.

A worked example. Over the last 14 days (with decay), A consumed 70 % of the billed GPU-hours and B 30 %:

LF_A = 0.8125 / 0.70 = 1.16 LF_B = 0.1875 / 0.30 = 0.625

A is under-served relative to its share, so it goes first: its users get the highest ranks. B’s borrowing jobs will wait until A’s usage is back to normal. B’s jobs in its owner QOS remain guaranteed (see QOS).

Measuring consumption: GPU billing

By default consumption is measured in CPU x seconds [2]. On a GPU cluster that is wrong: a job taking 1 core and 8 GPUs would cost almost nothing. So TRESBillingWeights is set on the partition [2], with PriorityFlags=MAX_TRES. A job’s billing then becomes the per-node maximum of the weighted TRES (CPU, memory, GRES) [2], not their sum.

The weights are calibrated so that a whole server is worth 8 units, whichever resource saturates it. For a server of C cores and M GiB of allocatable memory:

w_GPU = 1 w_CPU = 8 / C w_Mem = 8 / M

With C = 128 and M = 3072 GiB: CPU=0.0625,Mem=0.0026G,GRES/gpu=1.0. A job taking 1 GPU but 64 cores is billed 4 units, because it makes 4 GPUs unusable for others. The unit of account becomes the GPU-equivalent second.

To validate: replace C and M by the values of slurmd -C [5] on your servers (CPUs and RealMemory minus the memory reserved for the system).

Decay of consumption

PriorityDecayHalfLife is 7 days by default and applies every PriorityCalcPeriod (5 minutes by default) [2]. We recommend 14 days: training jobs on B300 often last several days, and a too-short half-life would erase a consumption debt before the other institution could catch up. PriorityUsageResetPeriod stays NONE: an abrupt reset creates edge effects at the start of a period.

Guarantee by QOS and preemption

The QOS

QOS Cap Role
instA GrpTRES=gres/gpu=G_A A’s share, never preempted
instB GrpTRES=gres/gpu=G_B B’s share, never preempted
service GrpTRES=gres/gpu=G_S shared vLLM instances, never preempted
borrow none surplus; preemptible by the three QOS above; ordered by fair-share

GrpTRES limits the total TRES allocated to all running jobs of the QOS [4]. Since G_A + G_B + G_S = 32, the sum of the guaranteed shares never exceeds the cluster. The GPUs an owner does not occupy are either free or held by borrow jobs, therefore recoverable by preemption.

Splitting between batch and inference

The inference service is a common good: its GPUs are taken from each share in proportion to ownership. With an inference pool of 16 GPUs (2 servers, 2 TP=8 instances):

Total share of which inference (pro rata) Guaranteed batch
A 26 13 G_A = 13
B 6 3 G_B = 3
Service – – G_S = 16

With a pool of 8 GPUs the pro rata gives 6.5 and 1.5, so it is rounded to G_A = 19 and G_B = 5: fair-share, which counts continuously, rebalances the half GPU over time. The inference pool can change size with the time of day (elastic pool); the GPUs released go to borrow jobs.

B’s big jobs: a weekly reservation

B’s guaranteed share (G_B = 3 or 5) is below 8. Without a special measure, B can run a job on a whole server (TP=8, multi-GPU training) only in the borrow QOS, hence with no guaranteed delay. B is given a recurring reservation of one whole server.

# A 48 h window every week, starting Monday 8:00, for institution B
scontrol create reservation ReservationName=instB_weekly \
 StartTime=2026-11-02T08:00:00 Duration=2-00:00:00 Flags=WEEKLY \
 Accounts=instB PartitionName=gpu NodeCnt=1

# On B's side, during the window
sbatch -A b_lab --reservation=instB_weekly --qos=borrow \
 --gres=gpu:b300:8 --time=2-00:00:00 training.sh

Slurm’s behaviour, from the reservation documentation [21]:

  • WEEKLY makes the reservation recurring: it activates and deactivates itself every week.
  • During the window, the reserved resources serve only the reservation’s jobs: “no other jobs can use those resources”.
  • Unused reserved time is charged to the reservation’s users or accounts, in equal parts. Here all of it goes to instB. B therefore pays for its window in fair-share whether it uses it or not. That is fair (the server was taken from the others) and it encourages reserving only what will be used.
  • B submits in the borrow QOS, not in instB whose 3-GPU cap would block an 8-GPU job. The preemption risk is nil: no owner job of A can enter the reserved server.

Sizing. B’s weekly share is 6 x 168 = 1,008 GPU-hours. A 48 h window costs 8 x 48 = 384 GPU-hours, 38 % of its share. The rest is consumed in instB and borrow. The agreement fixes the duration; a 126 h window would exhaust all of B’s share in a whole server.

Before each window, Slurm must start on the chosen server only jobs that finish before it opens. borrow jobs that declare a short --time then keep filling that server until the last minute. This behaviour is verified in the acceptance tests (test 9). For B, the job must also fit the window: --time less than or equal to the remaining duration.

Preemption

  • PreemptType=preempt/qos: the rules come from the QOS in the database [3].
  • PreemptMode=REQUEUE: the preempted job is put back in the queue. This requires JobRequeue=1 or sbatch --requeue [3]. SUSPEND is rejected: a suspended job keeps its memory, hence its 288 GB of HBM per GPU, and the owner QOS would recover nothing [3].
  • PreemptExemptTime: minimum run time before being preemptible [3]. We choose 30 min, so that a borrowed job makes at least some progress.
  • GraceTime on the borrow QOS: the delay between SIGTERM and SIGKILL [3], used to write a checkpoint. We choose 300 s.

Guaranteed delay. An owner job that fits in its QOS starts after at most

PreemptExemptTime + GraceTime + one scheduling cycle = 30 + 5 + 1 = 36 minutes

and in practice much sooner, since most borrowed jobs have already passed their first 30 minutes. This figure goes into the agreement between institutions and is measured in the acceptance tests.

Reference configuration

slurm.conf (excerpts) 

ClusterName=b300
SelectType=select/cons_tres
SelectTypeParameters=CR_Core_Memory
GresTypes=gpu
NodeName=gpu[01-04] Gres=gpu:b300:8 CPUs=<C> RealMemory=<M_MiB> State=UNKNOWN
PartitionName=gpu Nodes=gpu[01-04] Default=YES MaxTime=3-00:00:00 State=UP \
 TRESBillingWeights="CPU=0.0625,Mem=0.0026G,GRES/gpu=1.0"

# Accounting and enforcement of limits
AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu,gres/gpu:b300
AccountingStorageEnforce=associations,limits,qos,safe

# Priority
PriorityType=priority/multifactor
PriorityFlags=MAX_TRES
PriorityDecayHalfLife=14-0
PriorityCalcPeriod=5
PriorityMaxAge=7-0
PriorityWeightFairshare=100000
PriorityWeightQOS=20000
PriorityWeightAge=5000
PriorityWeightJobSize=0
PriorityWeightPartition=0

# Preemption
PreemptType=preempt/qos
PreemptMode=REQUEUE
PreemptExemptTime=00:30:00
JobRequeue=1

# Isolation
ProctrackType=proctrack/cgroup
TaskPlugin=task/cgroup,task/affinity

Reading notes:

  • select/cons_tres is required for sharing GRES (MPS, shard) [5] and for the preemption of heterogeneous jobs [3].
  • AccountingStorageTRES: declare gres/gpu and its typed variant, as the documentation recommends [6]. Declaring gres/gpu also enables gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil [6].
  • AccountingStorageEnforce=...,safe: a job starts only if it can finish within its limits in TRES-minutes [4].
  • The fair-share weight dominates (100,000); the QOS weight (20,000) breaks ties; age (5,000) prevents starvation of an old job.

gres.conf and cgroup.conf 

# gres.conf -- automatic detection through NVML
AutoDetect=nvml

# cgroup.conf
ConstrainCores=yes
ConstrainDevices=yes
ConstrainRAMSpace=yes

With AutoDetect=nvml, Slurm fills in the details of detected GPUs. The Gres= line of slurm.conf stays mandatory, and a node exposing fewer GPUs than announced goes to DRAIN [5].

ConstrainDevices=yes limits a job to the devices of its GRES allocation [7]. Without it a job could open another institution’s GPUs.

MIG (optional). For small inference or TP jobs, the B300s can be cut into MIG instances. Slurm manages them with AutoDetect=nvml on the nodes concerned, each instance typed by its profile [5]. Shards, on the other hand, do not partition processes on the GPU [5]: reserve them for uses inside one institution.

Accounts and QOS (sacctmgr) 

# Institutions: shares expressed in owned GPUs
sacctmgr add account instA Description="Institution A" Fairshare=26
sacctmgr add account instB Description="Institution B" Fairshare=6
sacctmgr add account svc_llm Description="Inference service" Fairshare=1 Parent=root

# Teams (example) under each institution
sacctmgr add account a_physics Parent=instA Fairshare=60
sacctmgr add account a_biology Parent=instA Fairshare=40
sacctmgr add account b_lab Parent=instB Fairshare=parent

# QOS
sacctmgr add qos borrow
sacctmgr modify qos borrow set Priority=0 PreemptMode=REQUEUE GraceTime=300
sacctmgr add qos instA
sacctmgr modify qos instA set Priority=100 GrpTRES=gres/gpu=13 \
 Preempt=borrow Flags=DenyOnLimit
sacctmgr add qos instB
sacctmgr modify qos instB set Priority=100 GrpTRES=gres/gpu=3 \
 Preempt=borrow Flags=DenyOnLimit
sacctmgr add qos service
sacctmgr modify qos service set Priority=1000 GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16 Preempt=borrow

# Attachment: owner QOS by default + the right to borrow
sacctmgr modify account instA set QOS=instA,borrow DefaultQOS=instA
sacctmgr modify account instB set QOS=instB,borrow DefaultQOS=instB
sacctmgr modify account svc_llm set QOS=service DefaultQOS=service

# Users
sacctmgr add user alice Account=a_physics
sacctmgr add user bob Account=b_lab
  • Fairshare=parent on an account attaches its children to the parent for the computation [8]: B, which has a single laboratory, adds no useless level.
  • DenyOnLimit rejects at submission a job that alone would exceed the QOS limits [8]. An 8-GPU job submitted in instB is refused immediately instead of waiting forever; the user is invited to use borrow.
  • svc_llm receives a symbolic share: its guarantee comes from the service QOS, not from fair-share. Its consumption is re-charged to the institutions (see accounting).

User side 

# Within one's guaranteed share (default QOS)
sbatch -A a_physics --gres=gpu:b300:4 train.sh

# Beyond one's share: borrowing, preemptible, must be able to resume
sbatch -A a_physics --qos=borrow --requeue --gres=gpu:b300:8 \
 --signal=B:TERM@300 train_checkpoint.sh

The script of a borrow job traps SIGTERM, writes a checkpoint within the 300 s of GraceTime, and restarts from the last checkpoint when requeued.

Monitoring

Command What it shows
sshare -l each association’s Level FS [1]: are A and B over- or under-served?
sprio -l decomposition of the priority of waiting jobs by factor
sreport cluster AccountUtilizationByUser -T gres/gpu GPU-hours per account over a period
scontrol show job <id> the PreemptEligibleTime [3] of a borrowed job

item.title: Inference: vLLM and the gateway
item.description:
Inference

Shared inference is vLLM running inside Slurm, behind a gateway that is the only HTTPS entry point. In the original design the gateway is LiteLLM; the measurements below are of LiteLLM 1.106.2. The Go gateway of this organisation implements the fair-share policy that LiteLLM’s free edition lacks.

vLLM in Slurm

Each vLLM instance is a long Slurm job in the svc_llm account and the service QOS. It is therefore accounted, cgroup-isolated, and never preempted. For a whole server:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -A svc_llm --qos=service
#SBATCH --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:b300:8 --exclusive
#SBATCH --time=7-00:00:00 --job-name=vllm-large-model
vllm serve <model> \
 --host <node-internal-ip> --port 8000 \
 --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
 --scheduling-policy priority \
 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \
 --enable-prefix-caching \
 --max-num-seqs 256 \
 --api-key "$(cat /etc/vllm/internal-key)"
Option Role (from the engine arguments documentation [9])
--tensor-parallel-size number of tensor-parallel groups; 8 = one NVLink server
--data-parallel-size replicas; for MoE models experts are spread over TP x DP
--enable-expert-parallel expert parallelism instead of tensor parallelism for MoE layers
--scheduling-policy fcfs (default) or priority: order by priority, then arrival
--max-num-seqs maximum number of sequences per iteration
--max-num-batched-tokens maximum number of tokens per iteration
--gpu-memory-utilization share of GPU memory given to vLLM (default 0.92)
--enable-prefix-caching reuses the KV cache of common prefixes (shared system prompts)
--kv-cache-dtype KV cache type (fp8, nvfp4…): more context in memory
--enable-lora, --max-loras per-team LoRA adapters on one base model

Per-request priority

A request may carry an integer priority: the lower it is, the sooner the request runs (default 0). The X-Vllm-Priority header takes precedence over the JSON body. Any non-zero value is an error if the server was not started with --scheduling-policy priority [10].

What the scheduler does, from its source code [25]:

  • the waiting queue is a heap sorted by (priority, arrival_time): the smallest priority comes out first, arrival breaks ties;
  • when a running request cannot find KV-cache blocks any more, vLLM preempts the running request with the largest (priority, arrival_time) and puts it back at the head of the queue;
  • a high-priority waiting request does not preempt a running request: it takes the first slot that frees up.

Priority therefore orders admission and designates the victims when memory runs short. It does not interrupt generations in progress. Since a generation lasts a few seconds, the effect on latency is quick. We use it to put interactive use (VS Code, chat) ahead of API batch processing, and for the split between institutions (below).

Securing vLLM

--api-key protects only the /v1, /v2 and /inference paths. Other endpoints of the same server, such as /invocations, are not authenticated. The documentation asks not to rely on --api-key alone and to put vLLM behind a proxy [10].

Hence the rules: vLLM listens on the cluster’s internal interface only; a firewall lets only the gateway reach the vLLM ports; the internal key is read from a file, never passed in clear in the environment or in shell history.

Prefix-cache isolation

With --enable-prefix-caching, vLLM reuses cached KV blocks across requests that share a prompt prefix. That reuse is a timing side channel between tenants: a caller can tell from the time to first token whether a guessed prefix was cached, hence whether another institution sent it (vLLM’s security guide; CVE-2025-46570). On a cluster shared by A and B this must be closed. The vLLM mechanism is the cache_salt request field, mixed into the hash of the first KV block. The Go gateway (v0.3.0) always sets a stable per-tenant salt (an HMAC of the tenant under a secret key file of at least 32 random bytes) and drops the client’s own; cache_isolation chooses the tenant (org by default, team, key, or none). Two limits to keep in mind: users inside one scope can still probe each other (team or key narrow it, at the cost of cache reuse), and cache_salt is not a hard isolation boundary, which only a vLLM instance per tenant is. Rotating the key empties everyone’s cache.

Elastic pool

At night and at weekends interactive inference drops. An scontrol update or a scrontab can stop one instance in two: 8 GPUs go back to the borrow QOS, without changing A’s and B’s guarantees. On the gateway side the second instance leaves the routing; its requests go to the first, which stays available.

The gateway

The gateway is the only HTTPS entry point of inference. It carries:

  • identity: a virtual key per user, attached to a team = an institution;
  • quotas: rate (tokens/min, requests/min, concurrent requests) and a budget per team;
  • the 81.25 / 18.75 split under saturation;
  • accounting: spend in tokens per team, the basis of the re-charging.
With LiteLLM, budgets are enforced only with a Postgres database. Without one they are not enforced at all [11]. With several LiteLLM instances Redis is needed too, or each instance counts on its own and limits can be exceeded. Enable fail_closed_budget_enforcement and fail_closed_rate_limit_enforcement: if Redis or the database fails, the gateway answers 503 instead of letting requests through uncounted [11].

Models and routing

This is LiteLLM’s configuration; the interactive group pins priority 0 and the batch group pins priority 10, on the same instances.

model_list:
 # Interactive group (VS Code, chat): vLLM priority pinned to 0
 - model_name: large-model
 litellm_params:
 model: hosted_vllm/<model>
 api_base: http://gpu01.internal:8000/v1
 api_key: os.environ/VLLM_INTERNAL_KEY
 extra_headers: {X-Vllm-Priority: "0"}
 model_info: &cost # internal cost, calibrated on the accounting page
 input_cost_per_token: <c_in>
 output_cost_per_token: <c_out>
 cache_read_input_token_cost: <c_cache>
 - model_name: large-model
 litellm_params:
 model: hosted_vllm/<model>
 api_base: http://gpu02.internal:8000/v1
 api_key: os.environ/VLLM_INTERNAL_KEY
 extra_headers: {X-Vllm-Priority: "0"}
 model_info: *cost
 # Batch group (API scripts): same instances, priority 10
 - model_name: large-model-batch
 litellm_params:
 model: hosted_vllm/<model>
 api_base: http://gpu01.internal:8000/v1
 api_key: os.environ/VLLM_INTERNAL_KEY
 extra_headers: {X-Vllm-Priority: "10"}
 model_info: *cost
 # (... same for gpu02 ...)

router_settings:
 routing_strategy: least-busy
 allowed_fails: 3
 cooldown_time: 30
 redis_host: os.environ/REDIS_HOST
 redis_port: os.environ/REDIS_PORT
 redis_password: os.environ/REDIS_PASSWORD

general_settings:
 master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY
 database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL

Two deployments sharing a model_name form a group, and the routing strategy spreads requests between them. least-busy picks the deployment with the fewest calls in progress. A failing deployment goes into cooldown alone, not the whole group [13].

Zero costs = budgets ignored. A model whose two costs are 0 is subject to no budget check [11]. The model is hosted locally, but it must still be given an internal cost, calibrated in GPU-hours (see accounting). Otherwise max_budget protects nothing. Costs are declared under model_info [22]. Measured on LiteLLM 1.106.2: without a cost, spend stays at 0; with a cost, it equals exactly 3 c_in + 1 c_out for 3 input tokens and 1 output token.

Teams, keys and limits 

# One team per institution (indicative values)
curl -X POST https://llm.example.org/team/new \
 -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/.config/litellm/master)" \
 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
 -d '{"team_alias": "instA", "max_budget": 1300, "budget_duration": "30d",
 "max_parallel_requests": 200, "metadata": {"priority": "instA"}}'

curl -X POST https://llm.example.org/team/new ... \
 -d '{"team_alias": "instB", "max_budget": 300, "budget_duration": "30d",
 "max_parallel_requests": 50, "metadata": {"priority": "instB"}}'

# One key per user, attached to their team
curl -X POST https://llm.example.org/key/generate ... \
 -d '{"team_id": "<instB-id>", "key_alias": "bob-vscode",
 "rpm_limit": 60, "max_parallel_requests": 8}'

A key that carries a team_id is governed by the team’s budget, not by its owner’s personal budget. The limits tpm_limit, rpm_limit and max_parallel_requests can be set on the team, the user or the key. For one per-model limit, the key’s wins over the team’s [11]. The budget resets at each budget_duration [11].

Do not pass the secret on the command line. The examples read the master key from a file readable by its owner only, never from an environment variable or an argument visible in ps.

Fair-share for inference: reservation by priority

LiteLLM’s dynamic_rate_limiter_v3 shares a model’s TPM/RPM capacity between teams. Below a saturation threshold anyone may borrow the free capacity. Above it, each priority is brought back to its reserved share [14]. It is a direct transposition of the Slurm model: lending of surplus, guarantee at saturation.

litellm_settings:
 callbacks: ["dynamic_rate_limiter_v3"]
 priority_reservation:
 instA: 0.8125
 instB: 0.1875
 saturation_threshold: 0.8

A key’s priority comes from its team’s metadata.priority, which wins over the key’s. Keys with no priority fall into a common pool (default_priority, 0.25 by default) [14]. The model’s capacity (rpm/tpm of the deployments) is measured in acceptance on your B300s, at the target latency.

(1) Priority reservation is marked beta and requires a LiteLLM Enterprise licence (30-day free trial) [14]. (2) Borrowed capacity is not taken back when strict mode engages, and TPM is checked at admission: a burst can exceed the limit. (3) With several LiteLLM instances, strict mode may engage late on a node that has not seen the traffic (60 s cache by default) [14].

What LiteLLM forwards to vLLM: measurements

The documentation does not say what reaches vLLM. We measured it on 23 October 2026. A real LiteLLM 1.106.2 was placed in front of a fake vLLM written in Go that records every request it receives: path, headers, JSON body. Control: a request sent directly to the fake vLLM with priority: 99 and the header X-Vllm-Priority: 99 shows up intact. So the instrument does see what it looks for.

Sent by the client to LiteLLM Received by vLLM
"priority": 10 in the body nothing: LiteLLM consumes this field for its own beta scheduler [15] (response header x-litellm-request-prioritization-used, +300 ms latency)
"extra_body": {"priority": 3} "priority": 3 in the body
deployment extra_body: {priority: 5} + client extra_body at 0 "priority": 0: the client overrides the deployment’s value
deployment extra_headers: {X-Vllm-Priority: "6"} X-Vllm-Priority: 6
same + client X-Vllm-Priority: 0, client headers forwarded [23] X-Vllm-Priority: "0, 6": values merged, no longer an integer
same + client X-Vllm-Priority: 0 and x-pass-X-Vllm-Priority: 1, default settings X-Vllm-Priority: 6: the client’s headers do not pass

Conclusion: the only safe configuration.

  1. Pin the priority by header in the deployment (extra_headers), never by extra_body.
  2. Leave forward_client_headers_to_llm_api disabled (the default).
  3. A client can still slip priority into the body through extra_body. But vLLM gives the header precedence over the body [10], so the pinned header wins.
  4. Do not use LiteLLM’s own priority field: it enables a beta scheduler that adds latency.

The class of service (interactive or batch) is then chosen by the model name (large-model or large-model-batch). The keys of batch scripts are restricted to the second.

Split with lending, without a licence

Free-edition LiteLLM provides keys, teams, budgets and static limits (tpm_limit, rpm_limit, max_parallel_requests) [11]. What is missing is the lending. Static limits at 81.25 / 18.75 leave an absent institution’s share unused.

The proposal is to reproduce the Slurm scheme (guaranteed share plus preemptible borrowing) at request level: a small relay between the gateway and vLLM counts the requests in flight per institution. Let C be the sustainable concurrency of an instance, measured (see accounting).

  • If the institution has fewer than p x C requests in flight (p = 0.8125 or 0.1875), the request is within its share: X-Vllm-Priority is 0 (interactive) or 1 (batch).
  • Otherwise it is borrowing: priority 10 (interactive) or 11 (batch).
  • The relay overwrites any priority and any X-Vllm-Priority coming from the client.

vLLM then does exactly what is expected (see priority): within-share requests are admitted before borrowing ones; when KV memory runs short, borrowers are preempted first. Without competition an institution takes everything; under saturation each gets its share back.

This is the policy the gateway (v0.11.0) implements in its fairshare package, with the two refinements the simulator forced (the reservation test counts within-share requests, and usage is charged at release). It replaces LiteLLM and the relay here: it holds the keys, organisations, teams and budgets itself, and the shares belong to the organisations (the institutions). For this cluster, its configuration (HCL2, not YAML) would be as follows, with the 256-request capacity of the gateway’s example. This block was run through llmflow-gateway check-config v0.11.0, with the key files present:

master_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/master.key"
cache_isolation = "org"
cache_salt_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/cache-salt.key"

org "instA" {
 share = 0.8125
 team "a-physics" {}
 team "a-biology" {}
}
org "instB" {
 share = 0.1875
 team "b-lab" {}
}

pool "b300" { capacity = 256 }

model "large-model" {
 upstream_model = "meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct"
 pool = "b300"
 class = "interactive"
 key_file = "/etc/llmflow/vllm.key"
 cost {
 input_per_mtok = 0.02
 output_per_mtok = 0.20
 cached_per_mtok = 0.002
 }
 upstream "gpu01" { base_url = "http://gpu01.internal:8000" }
 upstream "gpu02" { base_url = "http://gpu02.internal:8000" }
}

# the same upstreams again, with class = "batch"
model "large-model-batch" {
 upstream_model = "meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct"
 pool = "b300"
 class = "batch"
 key_file = "/etc/llmflow/vllm.key"
 cost {
 input_per_mtok = 0.02
 output_per_mtok = 0.20
 cached_per_mtok = 0.002
 }
 upstream "gpu01" { base_url = "http://gpu01.internal:8000" }
 upstream "gpu02" { base_url = "http://gpu02.internal:8000" }
}

The cost values are in GPU-hours per million tokens; calibrate them as in the accounting page. Note the gateway’s limitations, in particular one replica per pool.

To validate: how the relay knows the institution. Two routes. (a) One deployment per institution (api_base: http://relay:9000/instA/v1), reachable only by the team’s keys: safe, but one must check how LiteLLM exposes a single model name to two teams. (b) The X-Litellm-User_api_key_* headers that LiteLLM adds with add_user_information_to_llm_headers: we observed them (user id, key fingerprint). The presence of the team id could not be verified, because our test ran without a database, hence without teams.

Alternatives without a licence

Synthesis of each product’s official documentation, consulted on 23 October 2026. Y = native; P = partial; – = absent; $ = paid offer. Columns: keys and teams, rate limits, budgets, spreading between instances, reservation with lending.

Gateway Keys Limits Budgets Spread Lending Remarks
LiteLLM (MIT, Python) Y Y Y Y $ lending = Enterprise beta [14]
Bifrost (Apache-2.0, Go) [26] ? Y Y P – teams described in the free docs, but “governance across teams and customers” is listed as Enterprise: to test
Apache APISIX (Apache-2.0) [27] Y Y P Y – standalone YAML mode + Redis, no Kubernetes
Envoy AI Gateway [28] – Y P P – token-based limits; Kubernetes required
Gateway API Inference Ext. / llm-d [29] – – – Y P routing on KV cache; Kubernetes required; weighted fairness announced as “planned”
vLLM production-stack [30] – – – Y – router only
Portkey (MIT) [31] $ ? ? Y – key management is paid
Kong AI Gateway [32] $ $ – $ – advanced plugins are Enterprise

No free gateway natively provides lending with a guarantee. The only project that comes close (llm-d, weighted fairness) requires Kubernetes and still calls it “planned”. For a cluster without Kubernetes: free LiteLLM plus a relay covers the five needs without a licence and keeps the keys, budgets and accounts described here. Bifrost, written in Go, is an alternative to evaluate if its teams turn out to be free; the relay would plug into it the same way.

item.title: One accounting, in GPU-hours
item.description:
One accounting

Batch is counted in GPU-equivalent hours (sreport, after TRESBillingWeights). Inference is counted in tokens, per team (the gateway’s spend logs). They are reconciled as follows:

  1. Over the period (a month), read the GPU-hours of the svc_llm account: H_svc.
  2. Read each team’s spend in the gateway: D_A, D_B.
  3. Charge H_svc x D_A / (D_A + D_B) to A, and the remainder to B.
  4. Compare each institution’s total consumption (batch plus charged inference) with its share (81.25 % / 18.75 %).

Calibrating the internal cost

Goal: 1 unit of gateway spend = 1 GPU-hour. A saturated 8-GPU instance then “spends” 8 units per hour, and max_budget becomes a quota of inference GPU-hours, directly comparable with batch.

1. Measure the capacity. Once per model and per configuration (TP, KV-cache dtype), with vllm bench serve [24]. Use a mix of lengths representative of the real usage (for example 2,000 input tokens and 300 output tokens for a code assistant). Raise --max-concurrency up to the limit of the service target, for instance a p99 time to first token under 2 s:

vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions \
 --host gpu01.internal --port 8000 --model <model> \
 --dataset-name random --random-input-len 2000 --random-output-len 300 \
 --num-prompts 2000 --max-concurrency 64 --save-result

At the chosen concurrency C (which also serves the fair-share relay), read the output throughput T_out and the total throughput T_tot in tokens/s, printed by the tool [24]. The input throughput is T_in = T_tot - T_out.

2. Split the cost of an instance-hour. Prefill (input) costs much less per token than generation. Fix a ratio r = c_out / c_in, typically r = 4, and solve:

3600 (c_in T_in + c_out T_out) = 8
 => c_in = 8 / (3600 (T_in + r T_out)), c_out = r c_in

A fictitious example, to illustrate the computation (the real figures come out of step 1): T_in = 40,000, T_out = 6,000 tokens/s, r = 4. Then c_in = 8 / (3600 x 64,000) = 3.5e-8 and c_out = 1.4e-7 unit per token.

3. Tokens served from the prefix cache. LiteLLM warns that a model with custom pricing bills these tokens at 0 as long as cache_read_input_token_cost is not set (a warning observed at LiteLLM 1.106.2 start-up). Set it to about c_in / 10: these tokens are not recomputed, but they occupy KV memory.

Why not a cost per second? LiteLLM accepts cost_per_second [22]. But vLLM processes dozens of requests simultaneously on one instance: billing each by its duration would make it pay for the whole instance, and the sum would far exceed the real 8 GPU-hours. The per-token cost is the right model.

Recalibrate at each change of model, vLLM version or KV-cache dtype, and check once a month. The GPU-hours of the svc_llm account read from sreport should stay close to the month’s total gateway spend divided by the average occupancy.

Compensation

If, over a quarter, an institution consumed markedly more than its share through inference, the committee may correct the Slurm Fairshare values of the next quarter. Batch fair-share already rebalances by itself within the half-life window: compensation is only an exceptional adjustment.

item.title: Access from VS Code
item.description:
Access from VS Code

Two uses, two paths: the code assistant talks to the gateway over HTTPS; development and job submission go over SSH to the login node.

Code assistant: the Continue extension

Continue accepts any OpenAI-compatible provider, LiteLLM and vLLM included: provider: openai with a custom apiBase [16]. The configuration file (~/.continue/config.yaml on macOS and Linux, %USERPROFILE%\.continue\config.yaml on Windows; Continue configuration) requires the fields name, version and schema. Each model declares roles among chat, autocomplete, embed, rerank, edit, apply and summarize [17].

name: B300 platform
version: 1.0.0
schema: v1

models:
 - name: Large model (B300)
 provider: openai
 model: large-model  # model_name exposed by the gateway
 apiBase: https://llm.example.org/v1
 apiKey: ${{ secrets.B300_GATEWAY_KEY }}
 roles: [chat, edit, apply, summarize]
 defaultCompletionOptions:
 contextLength: 131072
 maxTokens: 4096

 - name: Fast completion (B300)
 provider: openai
 model: small-code-model
 apiBase: https://llm.example.org/v1
 apiKey: ${{ secrets.B300_GATEWAY_KEY }}
 roles: [autocomplete]
  • The key is the user’s virtual key, attached to the team of their institution: their consumption lands in the right share. It is referenced as a secret (${{ secrets.... }} [17]), never written in clear in a versioned file.
  • Autocompletion sends a request on every keystroke. Serve it with a small dedicated model (an instance of a few GPUs, or MIG) and set an rpm_limit on the key, or it will eat the institution’s quota.
  • contextLength must not exceed the vLLM instance’s --max-model-len.

Development and jobs: Remote-SSH

Remote-SSH reads the user’s ~/.ssh/config [18]. Target the login node, never a GPU node: GPU nodes are reached only through a Slurm job, otherwise the work escapes fair-share and cgroup isolation.

# ~/.ssh/config
Host b300-bastion
 HostName bastion.example.org
 User alice
 IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_b300

Host b300-login
 HostName login.b300.internal
 User alice
 IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_b300
 ProxyJump b300-bastion
// settings.json (VS Code, user)
{
 "remote.SSH.remotePlatform": { "b300-login": "linux" }
}

remote.SSH.remotePlatform maps a host to its platform [18]. The login node is shared by many users, so also enable Remote.SSH: Remote Server Listen On Socket in the Settings UI (the page cited names it only by that label). The VS Code server then listens on a Unix socket locked to the user instead of a forwarded TCP port. This needs a Linux or macOS host, disables connection multiplexing, and makes public-key authentication recommended (Remote Development troubleshooting).

The VS Code server consumes CPU and memory on the login node. Set per-user limits on that node (systemd cgroups) so that one session does not penalise the others. Do not run computation on the login node: go through srun/sbatch.

item.title: Identity with your federation
item.description:
Identity with your federation

On a cluster co-owned by two institutions, people already have an account at their own institution. The aim is that nobody needs a second one: A’s and B’s users log in where they always do, and the gateway learns from that login which team they belong to.

If the institutions are in a SAML federation such as RENATER (France) or eduGAIN, the piece in the middle is authn-bridge (go-authn/bridge): an OpenID Connect provider placed in front of the federation. People log in at their own university; the gateway, which speaks OpenID Connect, gets a token. The bridge and the libraries below are documented in go-authn’s repositories; this page only shows how the gateway is pointed at them.

user ──> their university (SAML, RENATER / eduGAIN)
 │
 v
 authn-bridge (OpenID Connect provider)
 │ token
 v
 llmflow gateway: sso (administrators), jwt (inference API) ──> vLLM

1. Register the gateway at the bridge

The gateway is a client of the bridge. This block is authn-bridge’s configuration, copied from the gateway’s README (it is not llmflow-gateway configuration, so check-config does not apply to it):

client "llmflow-admin" {
 secret_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/llmflow-admin.secret"
 redirect_uris = ["https://llm.example.org/admin/callback"]
 id_token_claims = true # the bridge's ID tokens carry no claims about the person otherwise
}

2. Point the gateway’s sso and jwt blocks at the bridge

Administrators log in through sso; users of the inference API present the access token through jwt. The groups the bridge returns are entitlements held to the institution that asserted them, so the role and map blocks match them. This block was run through llmflow-gateway check-config v0.11.0 (with the key files present, and organisations, a pool and a model alongside):

master_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/master.key"
cache_salt_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/cache-salt.key"

sso {
 issuer = "https://bridge.example.org"
 client_id = "llmflow-admin"
 client_secret_file = "/etc/llmflow/sso.secret"
 redirect_url = "https://llm.example.org/admin/callback"
 scopes = ["openid", "profile", "groups"]
 role {
 value = "llm-admins"
 role = "proxy_admin"
 }
 role {
 value = "b-lab-leads"
 role = "team_admin"
 team = "b-lab"
 }
}

jwt {
 issuer = "https://bridge.example.org"
 audience = "llmflow"
 type = "at+jwt"
 map {
 value = "b-lab"
 team = "b-lab"
 }
}

With this, a member of B’s laboratory who holds a token with the group b-lab reaches the gateway as a person of team b-lab: their requests count in B’s share, their budget and limits are the team’s, and the spend report names them. The value strings stand for whatever entitlements your federation really issues (for example urn:mace:... values); read them from a real token before writing the blocks.

Behind it, the gateway refuses alg: none and HMAC tokens, requires aud and exp, and answers every refusal with the same 401. See the Identity page for the details, for SCIM provisioning and for key rotation, and keep in mind its limitations: a person holding a token cannot be revoked individually before it expires, and SSO sessions live in one replica.

item.title: Security audit, acceptance tests, governance
item.description:
Security audit, acceptance and governance

Security audit

Surface Risk Measure
Shared GPUs a job reads the GPU memory of another institution ConstrainDevices=yes [7]; no shard between institutions [5]
vLLM unauthenticated endpoints outside /v1 [10] internal listening only; firewall: only the gateway reaches it
Gateway quota bypass during a Redis/DB outage [11] fail-closed options; Redis and Postgres made redundant
Gateway budgets inoperative on a zero-cost model [11] non-zero internal cost (accounting)
Keys leak through a URL, a command line or an environment variable files with mode 0600; Continue secrets; rotation; one key per use
Logs confidential prompts stored in the database disable message-content logging; keep only spend metadata
vLLM prefix cache timing side channel between institutions: a caller detects a cached prefix by its time to first token (CVE-2025-46570) per-tenant cache_salt set by the gateway (prefix-cache isolation); a vLLM instance per tenant if hard isolation is needed
Login node computation outside Slurm per-user cgroup limits; SSH access to GPU nodes reserved to jobs
Preemption loss of work of borrowed jobs GraceTime plus checkpoint; PreemptExemptTime
vLLM priority a client gives itself priority 0 through extra_body (measured, measurements) priority pinned by header; client-header forwarding disabled; the relay (or the Go gateway) overwrites
Header forwarding the client’s x-pass-* and x-* reach vLLM if forwarding is on [23] leave forward_client_headers_to_llm_api disabled
FP64 usage double-precision codes on B300 (10 TFLOPS per server) [12] usage rule in the agreement

Audit anchor. The Go gateway (audit log since v0.5.0) keeps a hash-chained audit log of every administrative change, with signed checkpoints. A log in the database that the operator can edit is only partly trustworthy: deploy the audit anchor on the same S3 or Ceph storage the cluster already has, in a bucket created with Object Lock, so that exported checkpoints cannot be deleted or rewritten, and check the log with llmflow-gateway audit verify --anchor export and a public key kept outside the operators’ reach. Without an anchor, truncation and rollback go undetected. The Audit and logging page states what remains open.

Guardrails (gateway v0.6.0). Prompts and completions can be checked before and after vLLM, on this cluster, without sending them anywhere: hide_secrets masks tokens and URL credentials (using gitsafe’s redact), pii masks or blocks personal data (e-mail, phone, IBAN, French NIR, cards, IP addresses) with go-llmflow/pii, and llama_guard and prompt_guard classify with a Llama Guard or Prompt Guard model served locally by vLLM on the cluster, as a model of class guard that clients cannot call. The classifiers see the already-masked text. A guardrail that errs or times out refuses (503) by default. The generic HTTP adapter is off by default: it exists only when written, and then only with allow_external = true, because it sends prompts and completions out of the site. This block passes check-config v0.11.0:

guardrail "secrets" {
 type = "hide_secrets"
 orgs = ["instA", "instB"]
}
guardrail "pii" {
 type = "pii"
 teams = ["b-lab"]
 action = "mask"
 actions = { iban = "block", nir = "block", phone = "log" }
}
guardrail "safety" {
 type = "llama_guard"
 model = "llama-guard"
 teams = ["b-lab"]
 action = "block"
 timeout = "2s"
 on_error = "block"
}

model "llama-guard" {
 upstream_model = "meta-llama/Llama-Guard-3-8B"
 pool = "guard"
 class = "guard"
 key_file = "/etc/llmflow/vllm.key"
 upstream "g0" { base_url = "http://gpu09:8000" }
}

(Alongside the organisations, teams, the pool "guard" and the other models.)

Chaos to play during acceptance. Kill a vLLM instance under sustained traffic (the routing must fail over); cut Redis (the fail-closed mode must answer 503, not let requests through); preempt a borrowed job in the middle of writing a checkpoint (the resume must read the last complete checkpoint); restart slurmdbd during a mass submission.

Acceptance tests: prove the guarantee holds

Every guarantee is proven by a test that could fail:

  1. B’s guarantee. A fills the 32 GPUs (13 in instA, 19 in borrow). B submits 3 GPUs in instB. Measure the start delay: it must stay under 36 minutes, and under 6 minutes if the borrowed jobs are older than 30 minutes.
  2. Negative control. The same scenario with the borrow QOS without Preempt: B must wait. If B starts anyway, test 1 was not measuring preemption.
  3. Cap. B submits 8 GPUs in instB: immediate rejection (DenyOnLimit).
  4. Fair-share. After a week in which B borrows heavily, sshare -l must show LF_B < 1, and A’s borrow jobs must go ahead of B’s (sprio).
  5. Billing. A job of 1 GPU and 64 cores must be billed 4: the billing= field of AllocTRES in sacct.
  6. Inference. Saturate the model with a key of A; check that a key of B still gets about 18.75 % of the throughput (with the Enterprise reservation, or the relay) or its static limit.
  7. vLLM priority. During saturation, a request of the large-model group (priority 0) must have a time to first token markedly lower than a request of large-model-batch (priority 10).
  8. Inviolable priority. Send to large-model-batch a request with extra_body: {"priority": 0} and a header X-Vllm-Priority: 0. It must stay processed at priority 10. Control: the same request sent directly to vLLM goes ahead.
  9. B’s window. One hour before instB_weekly opens, submit in borrow a 3 h job and a 30 min job. Only the second must start on the reserved server. At opening, an 8-GPU job of B must start immediately.

Performance. Compare throughput (tokens/s) and latency (time to first token, p50/p99) of vLLM behind the gateway with those of vLLM direct, at equal load. The gateway’s overhead must stay negligible next to generation; if it does not, increase the number of gateway workers before touching vLLM.

Governance

  • Agreement between institutions: shares (26/6), guaranteed delay (36 min), size of the inference pool, half-life (14 days), the quarterly compensation rule, and the possible reservation of a whole server for B.
  • Quarterly technical committee: real consumption against share, median wait times per institution and per QOS, preemption rate, inference saturation.
  • Change of shares (the purchase of a 5th server, say): change the Fairshare and GrpTRES values. No redeployment is needed.
